The term 'flat lower bound' is never defined. For N=8 the ring all-reduce lower bound is 2(N−1)/N × M / B = 245/2.5 = 98 s; 56 s is achievable only with in-network reduction (e.g., SHARP), which is not available on standard Ethernet.

The ring all-reduce sends 245 GB per rank, giving ~98 s (§9.3).' Or define 'flat lower bound' explicitly as the in-network-reduction lower bound and note it is not achievable on standard Ethernet.

quoted_clause: Used when a model split across nodes needs the full weight or KV cache locally.
observed: The sentence implies all-gather is a standard way to obtain a full weight tensor or full KV cache locally in distributed inference. In common tensor-parallel inference, weights and KV cache are deliberately sharded and each rank uses its local shard; all-gather of the full KV cache would usually defeat the memory-saving purpose. All-gather is used in some parallelisms and some weight-materialization paths, but the sentence is too broad.
correction: Rewrite: 'Used when a consumer needs the concatenation of distributed fragments locally; examples include materializing a full weight tensor in some tensor-parallel layouts. It is not the normal way to handle KV cache, which is usually kept sharded.'

verdict_fix: Qualify the bullet: all-gather materializes fragments (e.g. FSDP weights); KV cache normally stays sharded, not all-gathered.
verdict_evidence: ch09:18 claims all-gather gives 'full weight or KV cache locally'; ch09:192 treats KV as a separate one-time transfer and FSDP gathering as the weight path — full-KV all-gather isn't the normal case.

quoted_clause: PCIe Gen5 x16 peaks at ~64 GB/s, but a single all-reduce usually does not saturate the full link: in multi‑GPU topologies the traffic is split across multiple GPUs and multiple links, so one link rarely carries the whole transfer.
observed: The passage gives a correct per-direction peak but then offers a non sequitur: a link can be saturated while carrying only a fraction of the tensor. In a ring all-reduce, each link carries (N−1)/N of the tensor per phase, which is 87.5% for N=8, not a small fraction. The reason effective bandwidth is below peak is protocol/latency/contention, not because 'one link rarely carries the whole transfer.'
correction: Rewrite the bullet to say: PCIe Gen5 x16 peak is ~64 GB/s per direction; a collective distributes traffic across links, and each link may carry a large fraction of the tensor; measured effective bandwidth is below peak because of protocol overhead, latency, message size, and contention. Do not imply that splitting traffic across links is itself the reason a link is unsaturated.
acceptance_test: For N=2 and N=8 ring all-reduce, the revised text must correctly state per-link volume per phase and total volume, and must not use 'traffic is split across links' as the explanation for sub-peak effective bandwidth.
verdict_fix: Replace '~ns' with '~100 ns (load/queueing-dependent)' or drop the latency column.
verdict_evidence: ch9:28 '| Chip-to-memory | HBM3 (H100) | 3.35 TB/s | ~ns |' vs '~us' rows; ch9:34 caption claims latency figures are [1P][FACT] specs; HBM access ≈100 ns

quoted_clause: and by the ring model of §9.3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor.
observed: The statement is true only per phase, not for the whole all-reduce. Total per-link traffic in a ring all-reduce is 2(N−1)/N of the tensor. For N=2, the per-phase fraction is 1/2, but the total per-link traffic is one full tensor, which is why the preceding sentence says a two-rank collective can saturate the link. As written, the parenthetical appears to contradict that sentence.
correction: State explicitly: 'per phase, each link carries (N−1)/N of the tensor; over the full reduce-scatter plus all-gather, each link carries 2(N−1)/N. For N=2 that totals one full tensor per link.'
acceptance_test: Recompute the per-link volume for N=2 and N=8 and confirm the text matches both the per-phase and total values.

quoted_clause: A realistic *effective* throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node — the multi-rail effective bandwidth referenced in §9.2 and Fig 9.1) ... $T_\text{ring} \approx 2\frac{N-1}{N}\frac{M}{B_\text{eff}} = 2\frac{7}{8}\frac{140 \text{ GB}}{40 \text{ GB/s}} \approx 6.1 \text{ s}$ ... a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s ... $\approx 98 \text{ s}$
observed: The chapter makes directionality its central rule ('The bandwidth denominator must use the same direction convention as the counted bytes'), yet the two fabric bandwidths used in the worked example are never given a direction convention. 'Aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports' reads as a bidirectional aggregate (2 × 25 GB/s = 50 GB/s per direction, 100 GB/s bidirectional), in which case 245/40 = 6.1 s double-counts the receive direction and the correct value is 490/40 = 12.25 s. If instead 40 GB/s is per-direction (2 rails × 20 GB/s effective), the printed 6.1 s is right but the phrase 'aggregated' is misleading. The same ambiguity applies to 2.5 GB/s (25 Gb/s = 3.125 GB/s per direction; 80% efficiency gives 2.5 GB/s per direction, not bidirectional).
correction: State the convention in the same sentence as each figure: '40 GB/s per direction (two HDR rails, ~80% of the 50 GB/s per-direction line rate)' and '2.5 GB/s per direction (25 Gb/s ≈ 3.125 GB/s per direction, ~80% after overhead)'. Then add one line: 'the ring time uses the send volume (245 GB) divided by the per-direction bandwidth; equivalently the 490 GB send+receive total divided by the bidirectional aggregate.' Repeat the convention in the Fig 9.1 caption, which currently says only '40 GB/s for an assumed effective two-rail HDR path'.
acceptance_test: Every bandwidth number that appears as a denominator in Ch 9 carries an explicit 'per direction' or 'bidirectional aggregate' qualifier in the same sentence, and the 6.1 s / 98 s / 0.54 s trio reproduces under the stated convention.
verdict_fix: Add 'per direction' to the 40 GB/s figure and Fig 9.1 caption; Option C's direction already stated at ch9:108.
